issues.legal_issue: A judicial order rejecting an application must give reasons that disclose proper consideration of the issue.
material_facts: The High Court rejected the request to modify its earlier order but did not give valid, specific reasons for rejecting the expert committee’s recommendation or for refusing the requested modification.
The stated grounds, including preserving greenery and avoiding brisk activities, were unsupported by the facts concerning the proposed replacement of dilapidated structures.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s orders on the construction issue were unsustainable because they did not state valid reasons for their conclusions.
issues.legal_principle: Giving reasons is an essential requirement of judicial decision-making and a principle of natural justice; reasons promote transparency and fairness and show that the court applied its mind. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. Dhaniram Luhar, AIR 2004 SC 1794; State of Rajasthan v. Sohan Lal, (2004) 5 SCC 573; Raj Kishore Jha v. State of Bihar, AIR 2003 SC 4664; Vishnu Dev Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2008) 3 SCC 172; Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. Sales Tax Officer, Rourkela I Circle, (2008) 9 SCC 407; State of Uttaranchal v. Sunil Kumar Singh Negi, AIR 2008 SC 2026; U.P.S.R.T.C. v. Jagdish Prasad Gupta, AIR 2009 SC 2328; Ram Phal v. State of Haryana, (2009) 3 SCC 258; Mohammed Yusuf v. Faij Mohammad, (2009) 3 SCC 513; and State of Himachal Pradesh v. Sada Ram, (2009) 4 SCC 422.

predicates.appeal_challenges_judicial_rejection: A party appeals a judicial decision rejecting its application or deciding an issue against it.
predicates.application_or_issue_is_adversely_decide: The court's decision adversely affects a party's application or position.
predicates.court_gives_no_valid_reasons: The court does not state valid reasons that explain its conclusion on the issue.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an adverse judicial decision and the court gave no valid reasons for it, the decision is unsustainable.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not reject the recommendation of an expert committee on a technical matter without a reasoned basis for departing from the expert assessment.
material_facts: The High Court itself appointed a committee of experts from relevant fields to consider the museum’s environment and facilities.

The committee recommended exploring a separate building within the campus for visitor, exhibition, educational, research, and related facilities, provided the landscape and architectural setting were respected.
No allegation of bias, bad faith, or disqualification was made against any committee member.

The proposed building would replace existing dilapidated annexe structures, would be set away from the monument, and was not opposed by the relevant environmental, municipal, or archaeological authorities.
The High Court rejected the recommendation and later refused modification on grounds the Supreme Court found unsupported by the record.
The governing Act did not prohibit the proposed use of part of the campus; it provided for the trustees’ functions and for acquisition of property, subject to governmental control and supervision.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the refusal of modification was set aside, and the modification application was allowed; any construction had to be compatible with the monument’s architecture and ambience and must not disturb its landscape.
issues.legal_principle: Courts should normally be slow to interfere with expert opinions and may safely leave technical matters to experts familiar with them. The Court relied on University of Mysore v. C.D. Govinda Rao, AIR 1965 SC 491; State of Bihar v. A.K. Mukherjee, AIR 1975 SC 192; Dalpat Abasaheb Solunke v. Dr. B.S. Mahajan, AIR 1990 SC 434; Central Areca Nut & Cocoa Marketing & Processing Co-operative Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, (1997) 8 SCC 31; and Dental Council of India v. Subharti K.K.B. Charitable Trust, (2001) 5 SCC 486. It also held that courts interpret provisions of law, relying on P.M. Bhargava v. University Grants Commission, AIR 2004 SC 3478, and Rajbir Singh Dalal v. Chaudhari Devi Lal University, (2008) 9 SCC 284. The Victoria Memorial Act, 1903 did not prohibit the proposed campus use and allowed the trustees, subject to the stated governmental controls, to acquire property for management of the memorial.

rule.if: appeal_from_rejection_of_modification and court_appointed_expert_committee and no_expert_disqualification_alleged and committee_recommended_heritage_compatible_facility and proposed_work_replaces_dilapidated_structures and lower_court_rejected_recommendation_without_valid_reasons

predicates.appeal_from_rejection_of_modification: A party appeals a court's refusal to modify an earlier order.
predicates.court_appointed_expert_committee: The court appointed a committee of experts to assess the matter in dispute.
predicates.no_expert_disqualification_alleged: No party alleges that the committee members were biased, acting in bad faith, or disqualified.
predicates.committee_recommended_heritage_compatibl: The expert committee recommended a facility on the condition that it respect the heritage site's setting and architecture.
predicates.proposed_work_replaces_dilapidated_struc: The proposed work would replace existing structures that had become dilapidated.
predicates.lower_court_rejected_recommendation_with: The lower court rejected the expert recommendation without stating valid reasons for doing so.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns refusal to modify an order, the court appointed an unchallenged expert committee that recommended a heritage-compatible facility, the work replaces dilapidated structures, and the lower court gave no valid reason for rejecting the recommendation, modification is allowed subject to heritage compatibility.
